title: Who Signed, And In What
subtitle: Coronations were theatre; real power signed in blood not ink
imageCaption: There are a great many images of the capital. Not one of them shows anybody signing anything.
hook: The Ashford spirit said the coronations were theatre. Waluigi believed him and disliked doing so — and then the Crown Works accountants itemised the scenery.

plainSummary.point: The capital writes everything down except decisions.
plainSummary.detail: Twelve documents, and not one records a person choosing anything. They are stock sheets, transport dockets, rent bills and invoices. The decisions are only visible as the dents they leave in that routine paperwork.

plainSummary.point: A person was moved through the city as cargo.
plainSummary.detail: A restaurant stock sheet lists "exotic stock, one, ambulatory, do not ice" with the price left blank. A prison docket moves an unnamed detainee through three transfers in 31 hours and hands him to a private carriage with no destination written down. A sewer runner's sketch shows both errands crossing at the same junction. Three clerks in three unconnected offices each logged one leg of the same route.

plainSummary.point: One criminal charge is being used as a threat, not a prosecution.
plainSummary.detail: "Consorting with Anomalies" was charged 51 times in eleven years. Nine went to trial. Forty-two were dropped before trial with no reason recorded. In 1040, nineteen were charged and none tried. A charge dropped that often is not meant to convict anyone — it is meant to make people do something.

plainSummary.point: The coronation was staged, and the invoice proves it.
plainSummary.detail: The Crown's own accounts bill for imitation regalia and for a second signing table delivered to a private house. Whatever was really signed was not signed at the public ceremony.

plainSummary.point: Nobody in the capital helps for free.
plainSummary.detail: Every rescue in this file has an unpaid invoice attached to it somewhere. Assume the bill is still outstanding.

plainSummary.point: The Arrangement has a witness now, and he was shot at for it.
plainSummary.detail: A 955 BF account from a ceremonial guard: a Koopa in an unlocked cell shook Fawful's hand with three Mages' Guild hoods watching, a month before the assassination; after a Guild orb put Bowser down to applause, the Chamberlain told the Guild to dispatch of the guard who had seen it. The Guild has his small son and calls it protection. The file holds the night posting, the dead guard's letter to Fawful's bean shop, and the shop's own card.

background.kicker: the crime the capital is still covering up
background.why: The thirty days after Princess Peach's assassination on Highsun 1, 955 BF, with the Regency's cover-up under active construction. Most of the strange paper in this file traces back to that month.

background.kicker: the conspiracy this file is testing
background.why: The alleged coordination between elements of the Regency and the Mages' Guild that let the assassination happen. It rests on Toadsworth the Elder's journals, which the Regency calls forgeries — which is exactly why this file prefers documents to testimony.

background.kicker: the institution behind half the signatures
background.why: Custodians of arcane order, self-appointed. They track individuals with magical badges without always telling them, keep null cages and seem more interested in what the contained can teach them than in whether the containment is ethical. Read this before assuming a Guild signature means oversight.

brief:
**The short version.** The capital keeps mountains of paperwork and almost none of it records a decision. Twelve documents in this file, and not one of them shows a person choosing something. They show food, transport, rent, charges and stage furniture — and the decisions are visible only as the shapes they leave in those routine records.

That is the finding: **the capital's paperwork is arranged so that the moment of decision never lands in the file of the place it was supposed to happen in.**

Waluigi opened this file expecting the opposite. He wrote at the time that the capital produces speeches while the ruined houses produce evidence, and that the archive would never get a usable sheet of paper out of it. That was wrong, and the archive would rather record a retraction than quietly stop mentioning it. The capital produces enormous quantities of usable paper. It simply never writes down the part you want.

## What this file is arguing

Twelve exhibits, and the argument they make together is one sentence: *the capital's machinery is built so that the decisive act never appears in the record of the place where it was supposed to happen.*

Take them in the order the archive filed them.

A restaurant stock sheet has four lines of food with prices and a fifth line — **exotic stock, one, ambulatory, do not ice** — with the cost column blank. An Imperial movement docket takes an unnamed detainee through three transfers in thirty-one hours and releases him to a private carriage with no destination entered. A runner's sketch shows two unrelated errands crossing at the same junction under the lower capital, which means the sewers are not an escape route, they are a **corridor with regular traffic**.

Then the charges. Fifty-one Consorting with Anomalies charges laid in eleven years; nine tried; forty-two withdrawn before trial with no reason given. In the early years every charge went to trial and every trial convicted. In 1040 nineteen have been laid and none have been tried at all. And the wanted bill for Markop's father exists in two printings from the same plate, four years apart, with the charge line cut out of the block and reset half a point high — false witness, then consorting with anomalies. Same man, same reward, same plate, **new offence**.

A charge that is laid and then withdrawn forty-two times out of fifty-one is not a prosecution. It is an instrument, and the archive would like to know what it is used to obtain, since it is plainly not used to obtain convictions.

## The Ashford problem, stated honestly

The spirit said the coronations were theatre and that real power *signed in blood not ink*. That testimony is the reason this file exists and Waluigi has spent the whole investigation trying not to lean on it.

It is one copy of one account of one conversation, transcribed by a third party in a hand resembling Luigi's, unauthenticated, with no second hearer produced. As evidence it is close to worthless and the archive files it that way.

Which is why the Crown Works account matters more than the testimony does. Eighteen hundred and twenty-five gold for a dais, standards, gilt-over-base-metal display regalia, carriage and night working, settled in full with no query raised. And ninety-five gold for a **second signing table**, charged as a rehearsal item and delivered to a private address rather than the hall.

Waluigi did not need a spirit to say the ceremony was staged. The Crown's own accountants itemised the staging, priced the fake regalia, and then billed for a signing table that went somewhere else.

That is the standing rule of this archive working exactly as intended: an unfalsifiable claim from an interested witness, corroborated in the least glamorous way available, by somebody in an office who was only trying to get paid.

## What is still missing

The iron beneath the hanging tree has not been recovered and the survey sheets do not help as much as the file would like. A feature annotated *hanging tree* on the 1021 sheet, with a margin note about compasses; open ground on the 1038 sheet; no felling recorded between them. That is a discrepancy, not a location, and the archive is not going to pretend otherwise.

Waluigi's assessment: the succession thread will not be settled by finding the iron. It will be settled by finding out who withdraws the forty-two charges, because that person is the one deciding what never reaches a courtroom, and this file has now established that they exist, that they have been at it for eleven years, and that they have stopped bothering with trials altogether.

WAH.

threads.title: Documents sealed in iron beneath a hanging tree
threads.text:
Coordinates in the Thornwood, per the Ashford testimony. Still unrecovered — but the survey sheets now put a *hanging tree* on the 1021 sheet with a margin note about unreliable compasses, and open ground on the 1038 sheet, with **no felling recorded between them**. That is a discrepancy rather than a location, and the archive will not upgrade it until somebody walks the ground.

**In plain terms:** two survey sheets disagree about whether a tree exists, and no one logged cutting it down. That is a gap in the paperwork, not a map reference — the archive is not going to dress it up as a location until somebody physically walks the ground.

threads.title: Consorting with Anomalies is an instrument, not an offence
threads.text:
Fifty-one laid in eleven years, nine tried, forty-two withdrawn before trial with no reason given. Early years: every charge tried, every trial convicted. 1040: nineteen laid, none tried. And Kaelor's wanted bill was reprinted from the same plate with the charge line cut out and reset. Whoever withdraws the forty-two is deciding what never reaches a courtroom.

**In plain terms:** a charge dropped forty-two times out of fifty-one is not being used to convict anyone. It is being used to make people do something else. Find whoever signs the withdrawals and you find the person deciding what never reaches a courtroom.

threads.title: People leave the capital as freight
threads.text:
*Exotic stock, one, ambulatory, do not ice* on a restaurant stock sheet with the cost column blank; an Imperial docket releasing a detainee to a private carriage at the goods gate with no destination entered; and a sewer sketch where two unrelated errands cross at the same junction. Three separate clerks describing one route without knowing it.

**In plain terms:** three clerks in three unconnected offices — a kitchen, a prison, a sewer runner — each wrote down one leg of the same route without realising. People are being moved out of the capital as cargo, and the cargo paperwork is the only record of it.

threads.title: The signing did not happen where the ceremony did
threads.text:
The Crown Works account prices the dais, the standards and three sets of gilt-over-base-metal display regalia — and then bills ninety-five gold for a **second signing table**, charged as a rehearsal item and delivered to a private address. The Ashford spirit's claim that the coronations were theatre is corroborated by the people who invoiced for the scenery.

**In plain terms:** the Crown's own accountants billed for fake regalia and a spare signing table sent to a private house. Whatever was actually signed was not signed at the ceremony, and the invoice proves it more reliably than the ghost does.

threads.title: Every rescue in this file was billed to somebody
threads.text:
Three hundred gold for *compounding under duress*, invented on the spot by the Mages' Guild and never received. An inert dragon scale traded for six bags of spotted mushrooms with both parties recorded as satisfied. An empty canister returned with a prisoner whose kit was supposedly removed on entry. The capital does not refuse assistance; it prices it and then argues about the invoice.

**In plain terms:** nobody in the capital refuses to help. They help, then invoice, then argue about the invoice. Treat every rescue in this file as a transaction with an unpaid balance somewhere.

threads.title: The Arrangement has a corridor now — and the Guild was loved first
threads.text: Until this session the Arrangement was a dead chamberlain's disputed handwriting. Now it is a corridor with people in it: a Koopa out of an unlocked cell, Fawful's hand in his, three Mages' Guild hoods saying the Guild is already in place and will not act yet, and — a quarter of an hour later, in a hall that had just cheered the Guild for putting Bowser down with one orb — the Chamberlain telling the Guild to dispatch of the only witness. The thread is the order of those events. The Guild did not seize the castle. It was applauded into it, and the first thing the applause bought was a kill order nobody in the hall objected to. The journals say *the Guild provided the method, the Regency provided the opportunity*. The account shows the method being cheered and the opportunity being spoken aloud, a month early, by a man in a new suit.

leads.title: Recover the documents sealed in iron
leads.objective: Locate the hanging tree in the Thornwood and retrieve whatever is sealed beneath it in iron. Start from the 1021 survey sheet, not the 1038 one, and take a second compass.
leads.why: It is the only physical evidence the succession thread has ever been offered, and it was offered by a spirit whose other statements are unfalsifiable. Two survey sheets seventeen years apart now disagree about whether the tree exists, with no felling recorded between them, which is either a cartographic error or somebody editing the map. Iron and paper are falsifiable. Go and get them.

leads.title: Identify the third branch
leads.objective: Establish which branch of the succession the Ashford spirit meant by “broken at third branch,” and whether the break was an event or a procedure.
leads.why: Held against the Aurelian grafting page, *branch* stops being a genealogist's metaphor and becomes the same gardening vocabulary the Feyward uses for splicing a bloodline. If the capital's succession was grafted, the crisis has a mechanism instead of a mystery.

leads.title: Name whoever withdraws the Anomalies charges
leads.objective: Obtain the withdrawal instruments for any of the forty-two charges discontinued before trial and read the signature block. One will do.
leads.why: Forty-two of fifty-one charges withdrawn without reason given, and nineteen laid in 1040 with none tried at all. Whoever signs the discontinuances decides what never reaches a courtroom, and this file has established that they exist and have been at it for eleven years. A charge used forty-two times and prosecuted nine is not a prosecution; it is a lever with a handle, and the handle has a name on it.

leads.title: Trace the goods-gate carriage
leads.objective: Identify the private carriage that took an unnamed Toad detainee out of the goods gate at 22:05 with no destination entered, and the clerk of the Chamberlain who authorised the movement at 21:40.
leads.why: The docket, the restaurant stock sheet and the sewer route card were made by three people who did not know each other and describe one route between them. That route is still open. Eager came back off it; the archive has no reason to believe he was the only person on it, and the stock sheet's cost column is blank because somebody else was paying.

leads.title: Settle or contest the Mages' Guild bill before it is assigned
leads.objective: Either pay the eight hundred and seventy, or challenge the three hundred gold charged for *compounding under duress* as a line item with no tariff behind it. Do one of them in writing.
leads.why: An unpaid bill is a debt and a debt is transferable. The Guild invented that charge on the spot with an Archmage standing over a bench, which makes it contestable — but only while it is still the Guild's to contest. Once it is sold on, the party is arguing with a purchaser who was not in the room and does not care.

leads.title: Find out what is in the fat vial, and who filled it
leads.objective: Trace the vial the Koopa prisoner carried from the dungeon to the Bean Badge — through the shop card's 'bring the vial', Fawful's own description of the vacuum shroom going into Bowser by way of it, and any Guild or Beanish apothecary record of a vessel built to dose a Koopa King.
leads.why: The vial is the one object in the night that was built to go into somebody, it was on the Koopa's errand list before Bowser came through the wall, and the Highsun 1 record has Bowser dragged across a corridor unconscious a month later with nobody asking why he went down so easily. If the vial was used, the official murderer of Highsun 1 was dosed by the people who later accused him, and that moves the file from 'who held the blade' to 'who held the Koopa King'.

leads.title: Establish which Toadsworth gave the Guild the dispatch order — and why the brothers did nothing
leads.objective: Put a second account beside John Lee's for the hall after the orb: who stood where, which Toadsworth spoke, what Mario and Luigi were doing when a hood loosed a bolt at a ceremonial guard in front of them.
leads.why: The account calls the man 'the chancellor' and the archive reads him as the Chamberlain; the whole Loyalist case against Toadsworth the Elder would change weight if the son said it, and the Regency's defence of the Elder would collapse if a second witness puts the words in the father's mouth. And two heroes watched a kill order given and obeyed. Either they did not hear it, or Highsun 1 was not the first night the brothers were in the wrong place with permission.

leads.title: Name the dead guard with the bean shop's address in his coat
leads.objective: Match the palace guard who died in Bowser's fire with the letter in his livery against the palace roll for Efferd 955, the Regency's casualty list for the incursion, and the Bean Badge card's 'the guard' who had not decided.
leads.why: If the hall had one Toad holding the Arrangement's address it had more than one, and a name turns 'the castle was full of it' from Waluigi's reading into a roster. It also tells the file whether the Arrangement recruited palace guards or planted paper on them, which decides how much of the forty-seven minutes on Highsun 1 was consent.

leads.title: Find out how the Guild came to have Toad Lee, and where Marilyn went
leads.objective: Account for the small boy between the dining-hall table past midnight — with the chambermaid Marilyn — and the Guild's dawn statement that his son was 'being taken care of' and would not have to worry about being trafficked in their care; find the maid.
leads.why: The Guild volunteered the word 'trafficked' about a child it was holding, unasked, to a father it had shot at. A custody chain for the boy is a custody chain for the one hostage the Arrangement is on record taking, and the boy grew up to be a member of Disaster Inc. whose own file already has a lead open on his missing time. The maid is the last person on the record with him before the Guild, and nobody has asked her anything because nobody has found her.

exhibits.title: Kitchen Stock Sheet — Line Four of the Live Column
exhibits.secured: 15 Harvestide, 1040 BF · Gilded Octopus kitchens, taken during the raid
exhibits.onRecord: A restaurant stock sheet for the week ending 15 Harvestide. Five lines. Four of them are food, priced. The fourth line reads *exotic stock, one, ambulatory, do not ice*, and [[roll:3|the cost column against it is blank|every other line carries a figure. A blank in a priced column is not an omission, it is a refusal — the house could not enter a purchase price because there was no purchase.|a busy kitchen leaves gaps in paperwork constantly.]]
exhibits.analysis:
## The finding is the empty box

Waluigi wants to be precise about what this exhibit proves, because it is easy to over-read and the over-reading is unnecessary — the correct reading is worse.

It does not prove that the Gilded Octopus knew it was holding a person. The line says *ambulatory*, and a kitchen that intended to serve something would say so; this kitchen wrote *do not ice*, which is a husbandry instruction. The house was keeping him alive.

What it proves is that the house **did not buy him**. Line 3 is truffle at sixty gold the half-ounce, entered to the coin. Line 5 is wine at a hundred and forty. The kitchen is meticulous. And against the one line that is a living creature, the price column is empty.

A restaurant leaves a cost blank for exactly one reason: [[roll:4|the goods arrived without an invoice|goods without an invoice are goods that came from somebody the house is not willing to name in its own books — which means the supplier is either a friend of the house or a threat to it.|a supplier's bill can simply arrive late and be entered the following week.]]. Nothing else produces that gap in a book this careful.

## Who feeds the exotic stock

The kitchen note is the part Waluigi keeps returning to. *Feed once daily.* That is a standing instruction, and a standing instruction implies duration. You do not write a feeding schedule for something that is leaving tomorrow.

Set that against the transfer docket filed beside this exhibit, which has Eager leaving Imperial custody at 22:05 on the 14th. He was in the back room of a restaurant within the day, on a feeding schedule, in a kitchen that had entered no price for him.

So the sequence is: a prison released him to a private carriage at night, and a restaurant received him without paying. **That is not a sale. That is a delivery between two parties who are on the same side of a transaction that has no money in it**, and the absence of money is itself the interesting fact, because money is the thing that leaves a trail.

## What the archive is not saying

Waluigi is not saying the Gilded Octopus is a front. Waluigi has one week's stock sheet and no accounts, and the responsible position is that [[roll:5|one blank line is one blank line|but the blank appears against the only line on the sheet that could not be entered without naming the party who supplied it, and that is a pattern of one that is still a pattern.|a single document cannot establish a practice, and this one does not.]].

What Waluigi is saying is narrower and harder to argue with. The party recovered Eager from a back room. The archive can now show that the back room was **expecting** him, had budgeted nothing for him, and had written down how often to feed him. The rescue was a rescue from a schedule.

Eager's own account has him moved four times. This sheet corroborates one of those moves from the receiving end, in the receiver's own handwriting, which is worth more than the account of a frightened scout and Waluigi says so [[roll:4|without any disrespect to the scout|Eager's account and this sheet agree on the room, the day and the condition. A corroborated frightened witness is a good witness, and the archive should stop treating fear as unreliability.|corroboration on a detail does not make the rest of a traumatised account safe to build on.]].

exhibits.title: Transfer Docket — Three Movements in Thirty-One Hours
exhibits.secured: Copied from the movement office register, 18 Harvestide, 1040 BF
exhibits.visual: GOODS GATE · 22:05 · NO DESTINATION
exhibits.onRecord: The Imperial movement docket for one unnamed Toad detainee. Entered 04:20 on the 14th. Moved to the deep hold at 06:00. Moved to the goods gate at 21:40 on the authority of a clerk of the Chamberlain. Released to a private carriage at 22:05, [[roll:3|with no destination entered|the destination field is not optional on this form. An entry that leaves it blank has been passed by a clerk who chose not to ask, and clerks who choose not to ask have generally been told not to.|forms go out incomplete everywhere, every day.]].
exhibits.analysis:
## Nobody escaped from anywhere

The party's working account of the Eager rescue is a running battle across three locations. Waluigi has no quarrel with the account of the fighting. Waluigi has a serious quarrel with the *connective tissue*, because the party has been assuming that Eager kept being moved because he kept nearly getting away.

He did not get away. He was **signed out**.

Read the authorising column. Movement 1, warden's office — correct, routine, a reception-to-cell transfer. Movement 2, a clerk of the Chamberlain's office — and here Waluigi would like the reader to stop. The Chamberlain is a household officer. The Chamberlain's clerk has no standing whatsoever in a detention facility, and the movement office accepted the instruction anyway, which tells you [[roll:5|what the real hierarchy in that building is|the warden's office runs the prison on paper and the household runs it in practice. A clerk with no jurisdiction gave an order and the order was obeyed within ninety minutes.|it may simply be a clerk who was believed because he was well dressed and sounded certain.]].

Movement 3 is the one that matters and it is barely a movement at all — twenty-five minutes at the goods gate, then out, to a carriage, against a seal the movement office **could not identify and did not challenge**.

## The goods gate is the whole argument

Standing rule 6 is quoted on the face of the docket: departures go through reception, in daylight, against a named receipt. All three conditions were broken in a single transaction, and the breach is recorded in the prison's own register rather than concealed from it.

That combination is very specific. A corrupt release is hidden. This release was **written down** — badly, incompletely, but written down — which means the participants did not believe they were doing anything they would be punished for. They believed they were following a different rule than the one printed on the form.

Waluigi has met this pattern before, in the Feyward file, and it is the reason that file exists: a house with two rulebooks, one for the record and one for the household, and the household one wins. Here it wins inside an Imperial prison, [[roll:4|which is a considerably larger house|if the household instrument outranks the written instrument in a state facility, then the state facility is not the authority in the building, and the file's title question — who signed, and in what — is the correct question.|prisons everywhere run on informal accommodations; that is not a conspiracy.]].

## The name that is not on it

The seal is unidentified. Waluigi cannot name it and will not guess at it in a file that is supposed to be evidence.

But the archive can say this much: the seal was **not the warden's**, the movement office knew it was not the warden's, and the movement office released a detainee on it anyway at ten at night. Whoever owns that seal can empty an Imperial cell without giving a reason and without leaving a name.

That is a capability, and capabilities can be tested. If the reader wants one thing to carry out of this exhibit, it is that [[roll:6|the seal is reusable|whoever used it once at the goods gate has almost certainly used it before and will use it again, and the register keeps every impression. The register is a catalogue of everything this person has ever taken out of that building.|a seal used once at night may have been borrowed, forged, or improvised for the occasion.]].

exhibits.title: Route Card — Junction Seven, Used Twice in One Day
exhibits.visual: TWO TRANSITS · ONE JUNCTION
exhibits.onRecord: A runner's sketch of the thermal section under the lower capital. Two routes are marked on it in different inks: the extraction of Eager from the goods-gate end, and the passage to the apothecary stair for Dan's elixir. They were made by different people for unrelated reasons, and [[roll:4|they cross at the same junction|two parties who were not coordinating found the same navigable line through a lava sewer on the same day. Either it is the only navigable line, or somebody gave both parties the same directions.|a sewer has a limited number of passages; overlap is close to inevitable.]].
exhibits.analysis:
## Two errands, one corridor

On 15 Harvestide the party ran two entirely separate operations in the lower capital. Hjumpik went after a cure for Dan. A second effort went after Eager. Neither was planned with reference to the other; the accounts do not even mention each other.

They used the same junction.

Waluigi has drawn this out because it is the sort of coincidence that dissolves under a small amount of pressure and becomes a fact about geography — and facts about geography are the most reliable things in this archive, because [[roll:3|the ground does not have motives|terrain cannot lie, cannot be bribed, and does not change its story between tellings. Where a route physically goes is the one class of evidence in this file that nobody has curated.|a sketch of the ground is still only as honest as the hand that drew it.]].

## What the survey office does not have

The thermal section appears on no public sheet. Waluigi checked, because the first question about any route is who else has the map.

Two parties nonetheless located Junction 7, independently, within hours. The plainest explanation is that the route is locally known — to runners, to smugglers, to whoever moves goods under that quarter at night. It is not secret. It is simply **unrecorded**, which is a different and much more useful condition.

An unrecorded route is one that does not appear in a patrol schedule. Note where the red transit begins: the goods gate. The same goods gate at which, the previous night, an unnamed detainee was released to a private carriage against an unidentifiable seal. The extraction route out of the capital's prison quarter runs directly into a passage the survey office has never drawn, and Waluigi does not think that is [[roll:5|an accident of drainage|a facility whose tradesmen's entrance opens onto an unmapped passage has an exit its own records cannot describe. That is a design, whether or not anyone alive designed it.|older cities are full of undocumented works; nobody planned this, they merely failed to survey it.]].

## The heat is the corroboration

Both parties reported the heat at Junction 7 as survivable. Waluigi notes that it is not — the thermal section is called that for a reason, and a sustained passage through it should have produced burns that neither account describes.

There are two readings and the archive files both.

**One**: both parties are exaggerating downward, as people do about danger they got through. **Two**: the heat at Junction 7 is genuinely lower than the surrounding run, which would mean something is venting or cooling there, and a cooled junction in a lava sewer is a maintained junction.

Waluigi prefers the second, for one reason. Two independent parties made the same observation about the same twenty yards, and independent agreement on a physical measurement is the strongest thing an archive ever gets. [[roll:4|Somebody is maintaining that junction|and a maintained junction under an unmapped passage next to a prison goods gate is infrastructure, with an owner, a cost, and — somewhere — a maintenance account.|two frightened accounts agreeing about temperature is not a measurement.]]

The file's standing instruction: if anybody goes down there again, look up. Cooling leaves fittings.

exhibits.title: Kit Receipt — The Canister Returned Empty
exhibits.secured: Recovered with the subject, 15 Harvestide, 1040 BF
exhibits.visual: ISSUED FULL · RETURNED EMPTY
exhibits.onRecord: The kit receipt for one personal canister, issued to Eager and recovered with him. The reception record says his scout's kit was removed on entry. The canister [[roll:4|came back with him anyway|kit removed on entry and returned on release is normal. Kit that never appears in the property book and is nonetheless on the subject when he is recovered was never booked in — somebody let him keep it.|small items are missed by property clerks constantly.]], and it is empty.
exhibits.analysis:
## A very small object with a very specific story

Waluigi is aware this is the least impressive exhibit in the file. A canister. Personal issue, cheap, of the sort every scout carries and nobody records.

That is precisely why it is here. **The unimportant objects are the ones nobody thinks to curate.** The stock sheet was written by a careful kitchen. The transfer docket was written by a clerk covering himself. This canister was written down by nobody, and so it is the only thing in this session's exhibits that has not passed through somebody's judgement about what should be on the record.

Two facts, both physical.

**It was not in the property book.** Imperial reception logged the removal of his kit. The canister is not in that inventory and was on him when the party got him back. Either reception missed it, or reception saw it and left it, and Waluigi notes that [[roll:5|a canister is not easy to miss on a small Toad|which leaves the second reading: a reception clerk looked at a frightened prisoner, saw the one thing he had that could hurt somebody, and chose not to write it down. That is a person making a decision, and the file would like that person's name.|a hurried search of a small subject in a busy reception is exactly the search that misses a pocket item.]].

**It is empty.** Not part-used. Empty.

## What empty means

A canister of this pattern carries perhaps four seconds of discharge. Emptying it takes a sustained effort or several separate uses, and it cannot be done accidentally.

So somewhere between reception on the 14th and recovery on the 15th, Eager used everything he had. The party's account of the rescue describes him as recovered rather than fighting — the account of the back room has him unable to stand. Both things are true, and the sequence matters: he was **not passive throughout**. He spent his one resource before he ran out of ability to resist, and the archive can date that expenditure to a window of roughly thirty-one hours.

Waluigi raises this because of how Eager is being talked about. He is being filed, in conversation, as the one who got taken. The canister says he was also [[roll:3|the one who fought until there was nothing left in the tin|and the difference between those two descriptions is the difference between a liability and a casualty. The archive will be using the second word.|an empty canister proves discharge, not courage; it could have been emptied in one panicked squeeze.]].

## The one operational point

There is a practical finding and it is worth more than the sentiment.

If the canister was discharged in the back room of the Gilded Octopus, then somebody in that kitchen took a face full of it within a day of the raid, and that is a person with a visible, dateable, unmistakable injury. Nobody has gone and looked.

The archive's recommendation is that somebody should, because [[roll:4|a burned face is a witness who cannot deny being there|the injury dates itself to within a day and places its owner in a specific room. That is better placement evidence than the archive has for anybody else involved in this session.|kitchen staff turn over weekly and the burn would have faded before anyone thought to look.]].

exhibits.title: Writ of Summons — The Writ That Cannot Be Answered at the Door
exhibits.secured: 18 Harvestide, 1040 BF · served on Markop by mechanism
exhibits.visual:
SUMMONS
SERVICE EFFECTED ON DELIVERY
exhibits.onRecord: A writ of summons from the Oathbound Bench, charging Markop with Consorting with Anomalies, delivered by clockwork owl. Four clauses. The third makes non-attendance an answer. The fourth provides that the bearer [[roll:3|does not wait for a reply and cannot receive one|the Bench has built a delivery system with no return path. A summons you cannot answer on the spot is a summons designed to be obeyed rather than discussed.|using a mechanism is simply cheaper and safer than sending a person into the field.]].
exhibits.analysis:
## The delivery method is a legal instrument

Everybody has focused on the charge. Waluigi would like to start with the owl, because the owl is the part that was chosen.

A writ can be served by a person. Persons can be argued with, delayed, offered a drink, asked who sent them, and — critically — **persuaded to record that the subject disputed service**. That last one is the whole game in any court that keeps a docket. A served party's first defence is usually procedural.

The Bench sent a machine. Clause IV says the bearer is not empowered to receive a reply, which converts service from a transaction into an event. Markop has been served, the Bench's copy says so, and there is no counterpart record of anything he said in response because [[roll:4|the mechanism has no faculty for taking one|the Bench has removed the only moment at which the accused could have created a record of his own. Every document in this matter will now be a Bench document.|a courier that does not take replies is standard for a summons; a reply is supposed to be filed at the Hall.]].

Combine that with Clause III — non-attendance is itself an answer, and will be recorded as one — and the shape becomes clear. Markop has exactly two options and both of them are entries in somebody else's book.

## The struck name

The served copy has the presiding Justicar's name removed. The Hall's retained copy has it. The documents are otherwise identical.

This is the detail Waluigi will not let go of. Striking the issuing name from the served copy does one thing and one thing only: it prevents the recipient from knowing, at the moment of decision, **who is doing this to him**.

Markop believes he knows. The party has been told the summons comes from his old mentor. Waluigi notes that Markop believes this from the *character* of the instrument rather than from anything on its face, and Waluigi has now spent an entire investigation on the theme of people confidently reading a document as addressed to them personally. Kamek did it with a seal. The archive filed that as a cautionary specimen and it is not going to make the same error one file later. [[roll:5|The served copy names nobody|so Markop's certainty about the sender is an inference, not a reading, and the file must carry it as an inference until somebody produces the Hall's copy.|the style, timing and charge are together as good as a signature.]]

## What the charge does not contain

Clause II: the charge requires no complainant.

Waluigi has checked the phrasing against the Bench's own docket, filed beside this exhibit, and it holds. There is no injured party in this matter. No one has alleged harm. The instrument is self-starting.

A charge with no complainant cannot be settled by satisfying anybody, because there is nobody to satisfy. It ends when the Bench decides it ends — which the docket shows is normally by **withdrawal**, without reason given, in forty-two cases out of fifty-one.

So the realistic outcome of answering this summons is not acquittal. It is [[roll:4|a withdrawal on terms|and terms extracted in exchange for dropping a charge that was never going to trial are the entire purpose of laying it. The Bench is not prosecuting Markop. The Bench is opening a negotiation with a writ.|a withdrawal is a withdrawal; forty-two people walked away clear and Markop probably will too.]].

The file's position: attend, say little, and get the Hall's unstruck copy while inside the building.

exhibits.title: Bench Docket — Forty-Two Charges That Never Went to Trial
exhibits.onRecord: Eleven years of the Anomalies charge in one table. Fifty-one laid, nine tried, forty-two withdrawn before trial without reason given. In 1029–1033 every charge laid went to trial and every trial convicted. In 1040 to date, [[roll:3|nineteen have been laid and none have been tried|a charge that has stopped going to trial has stopped being a charge. Something changed in the middle of this table and the change is in the withdrawal column, not the conviction column.|prosecutions ebb and flow; a slow year proves nothing on its own.]].
exhibits.analysis:
## Read the columns in the right order

The instinct is to read the conviction column. Nine tried, nine convicted — a hundred per cent, which looks alarming and is in fact the least interesting number here.

Read the **withdrawal** column instead.

Between 1029 and 1033 the Bench laid four charges and tried four. The instrument was being used as an instrument: you were accused, you were tried, you were convicted. Unpleasant, but coherent.

From 1034 the two columns separate and never come back together. Laid rises — four, nine, seven, twelve, nineteen. Tried collapses — four, three, one, one, zero. The Bench is laying the charge five times as often and taking it to court not at all.

An instrument that is used constantly and adjudicated never has [[roll:5|stopped being a prosecution and become a procedure|the value of the charge is now entirely in the laying of it. Whatever the Bench wants, it is getting before the trial date, which means the trial date was never the point.|a rising caseload with a falling trial rate is what an overstretched court looks like everywhere.]].

## What the withdrawals cost

The registry note is bland and load-bearing: *a withdrawal is entered without reason. The Bench is not required to give one and does not.*

So forty-two people were accused of Consorting with Anomalies and forty-two times the Bench let it go, and the record contains no statement of why in any single instance. Waluigi has gone looking for the obvious innocent explanation — that the charges were bad and the Bench, on review, dropped them. That explanation predicts something this table does not show: it predicts the laying rate falling as the Bench learns which charges will not stand.

The laying rate rises. Nineteen this year, which at the current run-rate is more than the whole of 1029–1037 combined.

An office does not do more of something that keeps failing. It does more of something that keeps **working**, and the only thing this charge can be said to be doing successfully is [[roll:4|producing forty-two settlements the record does not describe|because if the charge achieved nothing, it would have been abandoned; and if it achieved a conviction, the trial column would show it. The value is being realised in the gap.|the value may be deterrence, which by nature leaves no record at all.]].

## Markop is entry fifty-two

This is the exhibit that tells the party what the summons actually is, and Waluigi wants the practical version stated plainly.

On the base rate in this table, Markop's charge has a roughly eighty-two per cent chance of never reaching a courtroom. He is not, statistically, in danger of conviction. He is in danger of being **one of the forty-two** — of an arrangement, unrecorded, made in a corridor, in exchange for a charge quietly going away.

That is the risk to plan against, and it is a different risk from the one the party has been preparing for. Nobody needs a defence. Somebody needs to decide, in advance and while calm, what Markop is and is not prepared to give.

Waluigi's last observation is the uncomfortable one, filed in plain sight per house rule. Markop is the party's most rule-bound member, and this instrument is specifically constructed to extract things from people who take instruments seriously. [[roll:6|The forty-two were not cowards|an instrument that only works on the compliant selects for exactly the sort of person who turns up when summoned. The Bench has been fishing in a pool of the law-abiding for eleven years.|forty-two people settling suggests forty-two guilty consciences.]]

exhibits.title: Wanted Bill — One Plate, Two Charges, Same Reward
exhibits.visual:
FALSE WITNESS
ANOMALIES
SAME PLATE · RESET LINE
exhibits.onRecord: Two printings of the same wanted bill for Markop's father, four years apart. Same plate — the border damage at the lower left matches. Same reward: two thousand gold. The charge line has been cut out of the block and reset, and [[roll:4|the reset line sits half a point high|the charge was physically replaced in a plate that was otherwise kept. Somebody preserved the reward and re-engraved the reason, which is the wrong way round for an honest prosecution.|a reset line is ordinary jobbing print repair and may mean nothing at all.]]. The first says false witness. The second says consorting with anomalies.
exhibits.analysis:
## The reward is the constant

Waluigi will state the finding first and then defend it, because it is short.

**The sum did not change. The offence did.** Two thousand gold, twice, four years apart, for two entirely unrelated charges against the same man — one a documentary offence about testimony, the other a status offence about association.

In any functioning system the reward is a function of the offence. Serious crime, large reward. These two offences are not of the same seriousness and could not honestly attract the same figure. The figure was fixed first.

Which means the bill was never really about either charge. It was about the man, and the charge line was [[roll:5|the field that got edited to keep the bill legal|a reward has to be posted against an offence. When the offence stops working, you do not withdraw the reward, you change the offence — and the plate is the evidence, because an honest reissue would have been reset entire.|a printer reusing an expensive plate is thrift, not conspiracy.]].

## The same charge, one generation later

Here is why this exhibit sits in Markop's session rather than in a file about his father.

The *second* impression charges Kaelor with Consorting with Anomalies. That is, to the word, the charge on the writ served on Markop by clockwork owl on the same day this bill was obtained.

Father and son, the same instrument, four years apart.

Waluigi is deliberately not claiming this is a family vendetta, because the docket exhibit shows the Anomalies charge was laid nineteen times this year alone and Markop cannot possibly be nineteen people. The charge is in general circulation. It is the Bench's tool of choice.

But it does establish something narrower and harder: the Bench has [[roll:4|used this instrument against this family before|which means the file on Kaelor is open, or was reopened, and Markop's summons is not the beginning of anything. It is a continuation, and there is prior paper.|two uses of a common charge against relatives in a small jurisdiction is unremarkable.]]. Somebody at the Hall of Judgment has a folder with the surname on it.

## What was wrong with false witness

The abandoned charge is as informative as the new one.

Giving false witness is falsifiable. It has a proceeding, a transcript, a witness line — this archive has an entire event record about Kaelor walking into an office and finding a two-thousand-gold warrant, and about the witness line that produced it. A false-witness charge can be **beaten**, because it points at a specific statement on a specific day.

Consorting with Anomalies points at nothing. It has no complainant, per the writ's own second clause. It cannot be disproved because it does not assert an event.

So the edit is an upgrade in exactly one respect: the second charge is unanswerable. Somebody looked at a charge that could be fought and replaced it, on the same plate, under the same reward, with one that cannot.

Waluigi's instruction to the party is one sentence. When Markop stands in the Hall of Judgment, [[roll:6|he is not answering his own summons|he is answering the second impression of his father's bill, and the Bench will have both in front of it while he speaks. He should walk in knowing that. It changes what he should say.|the two matters are legally distinct and the Bench will treat them as such.]].

exhibits.title: Requisition and Charge — Three Hundred Gold for Being Stood Over
exhibits.onRecord: The Mages' Guild bill for Dan's restorative. Four hundred and fifty for the compound, a hundred and twenty for out-of-hours bench time, zero for the dragon scale because Hjumpik supplied it — and three hundred gold for *compounding under duress*, a line item the Guild appears to have invented on the spot. Total eight hundred and seventy. [[roll:4|Received: nothing|the Guild wrote the entire bill off rather than send collections after a dwarf. An institution that prices its own humiliation and then declines to collect has told you exactly what it is afraid of.|writing off an uncollectable debt at a bad address is routine accounting.]].
exhibits.analysis:
## An institution pricing its own dignity

Waluigi has read a great many invoices in the course of this archive and has never encountered a line quite like the fourth one.

*Compounding under duress — surcharge — discretion of the bench — 300 gp.*

That is not a cost. Nothing was consumed. No additional reagent was used, no extra hour was worked; the out-of-hours time is already billed separately at line three. The three hundred gold is the Guild attaching a **price to having been made to do something**, entered in a ledger, in a book that goes to an auditor.

This is the boring-document principle at its purest, and it is why the file prefers accounting to testimony. Nobody at the Guild would ever say aloud that a dwarf stood in their compounding room until they gave in. The bench wrote it down, in a priced column, because [[roll:3|a ledger has to balance and a grievance does not|the bench needed an entry to explain an out-of-schedule compound to whoever reviews the book. Explaining it honestly was easier than falsifying it, and so the Guild has certified the party's account of the evening in its own hand.|a discretionary surcharge is a standard catch-all line in professional billing.]].

## The write-off is the confession

Eight hundred and seventy gold is a serious sum. The Guild is not a charity; this archive has a whole event record about the Guild repossessing a *heal*, from a patient, mid-recovery, over money.

And this bill was referred to collections, and collections declined.

The stated grounds are worth quoting exactly: address unknown, temperament known.

The first half is boilerplate. The second half is a collections clerk writing, in a formal recovery note, that the debtor is too frightening to approach. Waluigi would like to note the asymmetry: the same institution that will take a healing back out of a wounded body will not walk across the capital to invoice Hjumpik.

So the Guild's actual policy is not *we always collect*. It is [[roll:5|we always collect from people who cannot come back|which makes the Guild's behaviour perfectly predictable and therefore perfectly exploitable. It is not a rule about money. It is a rule about consequences, and the party has now demonstrated it can supply consequences.|an unrecoverable debt is written off by every business on earth; this is bookkeeping, not fear.]].

## The zero that matters

Line two, reagent, supplied by applicant, zero gold.

The scale came from the dragon. The barter note filed beside this exhibit records what it cost: six bags of spotted mushrooms, which the dragon considered a fine trade and which are a controlled reagent below the capital.

So the true cost of Dan's cure was not eight hundred and seventy gold, and it was not nothing. It was six bags of a restricted substance, handed to a dragon, off the books, [[roll:4|and then not entered anywhere on the Guild's side either|the Guild recorded a reagent of significant value as costing zero because the applicant brought it. The transaction that actually paid for this cure appears in no institutional record at all. Only the archive has both halves.|the Guild only prices what it supplies; that is how requisitions work everywhere.]].

Dan is well. Waluigi files that first because it is the thing that matters. But the file should also record that the party has learned it can obtain restricted goods, convert them into a dragon's cooperation, and convert that into a compound the Guild would not otherwise have made — and that the entire chain is invisible to every institution that touched it.

exhibits.title: Barter Note — Both Parties Recorded as Satisfied
exhibits.secured: 16 Harvestide, 1040 BF · reverse of a ration chit
exhibits.visual: SIX BAGS · ONE SCALE
exhibits.onRecord: A barter note in a large unsteady hand, pressed hard enough to emboss the front of the chit. One shed shoulder scale, aged and therefore inert, against six bags of spotted mushrooms. The dragon records itself as having got the better of the deal because [[roll:3|the spotted kind is better and the dwarf did not know this|the dragon believed it was exploiting ignorance. It was recording, in its own hand, that it knowingly took a controlled reagent in trade — which is the admission, not the mushrooms.|a dragon boasting about a trade is a dragon boasting; the note proves an opinion, not an offence.]].
exhibits.analysis:
## The most honest document in the file

Every other exhibit in this investigation was written by somebody managing an impression. The kitchen was covering a supplier. The prison clerk was covering himself. The Guild was justifying an entry. The Bench struck its own name off a writ.

This one was written by a party with no conception that it might ever be read by a third person, and it is consequently the only document here that Waluigi trusts completely. It even boasts. *Good trade for me.*

An archive should be honest about the hierarchy of its sources, and the top of that hierarchy is not the sworn statement. It is [[roll:4|the note written by somebody who thought the transaction was over|nobody curates a record they believe is finished. The dragon wrote down the part it was pleased about, and the part it was pleased about happens to be the part that establishes what changed hands.|a boastful note is exactly the kind of source that inflates its own cleverness.]].

## What actually crossed the table

**Given by the dragon**: one shoulder scale, shed, aged. Waluigi has confirmed with the Guild counterfoil that it was accepted as a reagent and priced at zero because the applicant supplied it. Aged and shed means inert, which means legal to hold. There is no offence in the scale.

**Given by Hjumpik**: six bags of spotted mushrooms, described by him — per the dragon's note — as useless.

The spotted variety is a controlled reagent below the capital. Six bags is not a pocketful; it is a quantity that requires carrying.

So the trade was: a legal object, given by the party who thought it was overpaying, against a restricted object, given by the party who thought it was worthless. Both walked away convinced they had won.

Waluigi's assessment, and the file will stand behind it: **they had both won.** Hjumpik got a cure for Dan out of something he was carrying and did not value. The dragon got six bags of a substance it correctly valued and cannot easily buy. This is what a good trade looks like and it is rarer than the archive's usual subject matter suggests.

## The exposure nobody has looked at

The finding, however, is not about the trade. It is about where the mushrooms went.

Six bags of a controlled reagent are now in the possession of a dragon below the capital, obtained from a member of this party, evidenced by a note **in the dragon's own handwriting** that names the transaction and expresses satisfaction with it.

If anybody ever wants to establish that Hjumpik supplied restricted goods in the lower capital, they do not need a witness. They need this chit, and the dragon is keeping it, because the dragon is proud of it.

That is the practical finding and Waluigi would like it acted on rather than admired: [[roll:5|the evidence of the offence is in the hands of the counterparty|and the counterparty is senile, talkative, and entirely unaware that it is holding an exhibit. It will show that note to anyone who asks about the trade.|a barter note in a sewer is not going to end up in front of a bench.]].

Set against the Anomalies docket in the session above — a Bench that lays charges it never tries, in order to obtain unrecorded settlements — a signed admission sitting in a cave under the capital is not a curiosity. It is [[roll:4|leverage waiting to be picked up|and the party has now generated, in one week, exactly the kind of unanswerable material the Hall of Judgment has spent eleven years collecting from people.|nobody is going to connect a dragon's scrawl to a courtroom.]].

exhibits.title: Testimony — The Only Account, Taken at One Remove
exhibits.onRecord: The Ashford spirit's statement, transcribed by a third party in a hand resembling Luigi's and not authenticated as his. Three claims: the coronations were theatre, real power signed in blood not ink, and what was signed is sealed in iron beneath the hanging tree in the Thornwood. No second hearer has been produced, so [[roll:4|the archive holds one copy of one account of one conversation|which is the weakest possible evidentiary position, and the file's entire succession thread currently rests on it. Waluigi is putting that sentence at the top rather than the bottom.|relayed testimony is how most historical record reaches an archive; this is normal.]].
exhibits.analysis:
## Filed under protest, and filed anyway

Waluigi objects to this entire class of evidence. A dead man's statement, taken down by an unidentified hand, with no corroborating hearer, is exactly the material this archive was built to be sceptical of.

It is filed regardless, and the reasoning is a house rule worth stating: refusing to file the only testimony you have is not scepticism, it is squeamishness. The correct handling is to file it, mark its weakness on its face, and then **test the parts that can be tested**.

Two of the three claims are untestable. The third is not, and that is where this file's work is.

## Theatre has a budget

*The coronations were theatre.*

Everybody who has read this line has read it as contempt — coronations were hollow, the ceremony meant nothing. That reading is available and Waluigi thinks it is the lazy one.

Take the word literally. Theatre is a production. Productions have **suppliers**. A dais is hired, standards are embroidered, regalia is fabricated, carriage is charged, and every one of those things generates an invoice that goes to somebody's accounts department and sits there for years being profoundly uninteresting to everyone.

Waluigi went and found the invoice. It is filed as the last exhibit in this session, and it contains a second signing table delivered to a private address on the night before the ceremony. The spirit's sneer produced [[roll:5|a testable prediction that turned out to be correct|the testimony said the ceremony was staged; the staging account shows a signing table charged as a rehearsal item and sent to a house. The unfalsifiable witness has been corroborated by a furniture bill.|finding a stray item on a large ceremonial account is not corroboration of anything.]].

That does not make the spirit reliable. It makes one specific sentence of the spirit's productive, which is all the archive ever asks of a source.

## Blood not ink, read as a filing instruction

*Real power signed in blood not ink.*

Two readings, and the archive files both per house rule.

**Figurative**: settlements enforced by violence. Common phrasing, means little, cannot be pursued.

**Literal**: an instrument executed in blood. Waluigi is obliged to note that this is a documentary form with physical properties — it degrades, it is legible under the right light for a surprisingly long time, and it is the sort of thing one would store in a sealed container because [[roll:3|iron is what you use when the document itself is perishable|the container is the tell. Nobody seals ordinary parchment in iron. Sealing in iron is what you do for something that will rot, or something that will be sought.|iron chests are simply what secure documents were kept in.]].

The archive's preference — stated openly, as required — is the literal reading, on the single ground that the literal reading explains the iron and the figurative reading does not.

## The one thing to actually do

The Thornwood survey extract, filed next in this session, shows the hanging tree present on the 1021 sheet and absent from the 1038 sheet, with no felling recorded, and a marginal note that the compass is unreliable within thirty paces.

A ferrous mass in the ground produces exactly that effect.

So the spirit's least verifiable claim has a physical signature, and the signature is on a government map that predates the testimony by nineteen years. Nobody has gone and stood there with a compass. [[roll:4|That is the cheapest experiment in this entire archive|one person, one compass, thirty paces, and the succession thread either becomes evidence or stops consuming the file's attention. It costs a walk.|a compass deviation would only tell you there is iron, not whose iron or what is in it.]]

exhibits.title: Survey Extract — The Tree That Left the Second Draft
exhibits.secured: Survey office comparison, obtained 19 Harvestide, 1040 BF
exhibits.visual: 1021 SHEET · 1038 SHEET · ONE FEATURE GONE
exhibits.onRecord: Two survey sheets of the same quarter of the Thornwood, seventeen years apart. The 1021 sheet carries a feature annotated *hanging tree*, with a margin note reading *compass unreliable within thirty paces*. The 1038 sheet shows open ground. [[roll:3|No felling is recorded between them|the survey office removes a feature when it is gone and records why. A feature that vanishes between drafts with no felling entry was not removed from the forest, it was removed from the map.|forest surveys are re-walked by different surveyors and small features drop out constantly.]].
exhibits.analysis:
## What a survey office is for

A survey office is the least imaginative institution in any kingdom, and that is its virtue. It walks the ground, it draws what is there, and when something changes it records the change and the reason. Fellings are recorded. Fires are recorded. Land slips are recorded.

This feature is on the 1021 sheet and off the 1038 sheet, and between the two there is no entry of any kind.

There are only three ways that happens. The tree fell down and nobody logged it. The second surveyor missed it. Or [[roll:5|the second sheet was drawn to a brief|a survey is corrected against the previous sheet before publication precisely so that features do not silently disappear. Silent disappearance is not an error mode this process produces by accident.|a re-walk by a different surveyor in dense woodland absolutely can drop a single tree.]].

Waluigi is not going to pretend the first two are impossible. Waluigi is going to note that a hanging tree is a landmark, that landmarks are the load-bearing content of a woodland sheet, and that a surveyor who missed one would have produced a sheet that failed its own internal checks against the previous edition.

## The margin note is the exhibit

Strip away the testimony and the missing tree, and one thing on these two sheets is a physical measurement made by a professional who had no idea it would ever matter.

*Compass unreliable within thirty paces.*

That is a surveyor recording an instrument fault at a specific location in 1021 — nineteen years before a spirit said anything to anybody about iron. The note exists in a context with no motive. Nobody wrote it to support a story, because there was no story yet.

A local compass deviation of that radius means a ferrous mass. Not a nail, not a horseshoe — thirty paces requires **bulk iron**, in the ground, in quantity, at a spot that a separate and much later source independently identifies as the place where documents were sealed in iron.

Waluigi wants to be careful here, because this is the strongest inference in the file and strong inferences are where archives embarrass themselves. The correct statement is: [[roll:4|two unrelated sources point at one location|a 1021 instrument note and a relayed spirit testimony agree on a place, and neither could have influenced the other. That is not proof of contents, but it is proof that the location is real and anomalous.|a compass fault and a ghost story can point at the same tree for entirely unconnected reasons.]].

It is not evidence that anything is buried there. It is evidence that **something ferrous is there**, and that somebody removed the marker for it from the public map.

## The order of operations

The file's instruction, in order, because doing these out of order wastes the opportunity.

First, the compass. One person, one instrument, thirty paces, an afternoon. This costs nothing and either confirms the anomaly or ends the thread permanently, and Waluigi would be genuinely content with either outcome.

Second — and only if the compass confirms — the ground. Waluigi notes without enthusiasm that the party's instinct will be to dig immediately, and that digging first destroys the only clean measurement available.

Third, the survey office itself. Somebody authorised the 1038 sheet. Sheets are signed off. [[roll:6|The signature on the second sheet is recoverable|and it is a name attached, in writing, to the removal of a landmark that a compass says is still there. That is the only person in this thread who can be shown to have done something deliberate.|survey sign-offs from 1038 will be a clerk's initials at best.]].

One tree, three exhibits, and none of them require believing a ghost.

exhibits.title: Staging Account — The Second Signing Table
exhibits.secured: Crown Works account, obtained from the Chamberlain's office ledgers
exhibits.visual: PAID IN FULL · NO QUERY RAISED
exhibits.onRecord: The Crown Works account for a coronation season. A dais, twenty-four standards, three sets of display regalia in gilt over base metal, carriage and night working — eighteen hundred and twenty-five gold, settled in full with no query raised. And one line, ninety-five gold, for a second signing table, charged as a rehearsal item and [[roll:4|delivered to a private address rather than the hall|a rehearsal table is used where the rehearsal is. This one went to a house, the night before, and Crown Works never invoiced for its return.|properties are delivered to all sorts of addresses during a large production.]].
exhibits.analysis:
## This is the exhibit that opens the file

This investigation was not going to be opened at all until somebody brought back a sheet of paper from the capital. This is the paper, and Waluigi is aware of how it looks: a furniture bill.

That is the point. The capital produces speeches; speeches are curated. It also produces **accounts**, and nobody curates an account, because nobody expects an archivist to read one. This account was paid in full with no query raised, which means it passed through the Chamberlain's office without a single person objecting to any line on it.

Including line four.

## Three sets of regalia for one ceremony

Take the smaller finding first, because it establishes the habit.

The account charges for three sets of display regalia, gilt over base metal. A coronation requires one. The account does not say what became of the other two, and Crown Works — which invoices for the return of hired items, as the dais line shows — did not invoice for their return.

So two sets of convincing fake regalia were manufactured, paid for out of the ceremonial budget, and left the process without a destination.

Waluigi notes the material specification: gilt over base metal. That is a specification for something meant to be **seen and not handled**, at a distance, by people who will not weigh it. Which is a reasonable specification for a ceremony, and also [[roll:5|a reasonable specification for a ceremony held somewhere else|regalia that only has to survive a glance is regalia for an audience that will not be permitted close. Two spare sets and no return record is two more occasions that could be staged.|spares are ordered for every large ceremony because things get dropped.]].

## The table is the finding

Ninety-five gold. The cheapest significant line on the sheet.

A signing table is not scenery. It is the piece of furniture on which the instrument is executed — the single object in the entire production whose whole function is to be the place where a name goes onto a document.

Crown Works built two. One went to the hall. One was charged as *rehearsal* and delivered to a private address on the night before, and never came back.

Waluigi has considered the innocent reading seriously and it does not survive contact with the other lines. Rehearsals happen where the ceremony happens; the dais was hired for three days precisely so it could be rehearsed on. There was no rehearsal at a private house, because the dais was in the hall.

What there was, at a private address, on the night before a coronation, was **a table built for signing, and nobody watching**. Set that against the Ashford testimony filed one session above — the coronations were theatre, real power signed in blood not ink — and the two documents agree without ever having met. [[roll:6|One signing had an audience and one did not|and the one with the audience was the one on the hired dais, in front of the standards, using the gilt regalia. The account describes the set. The spirit described the play.|a stray property delivery is not the second half of a conspiracy.]]

## What to ask for next

The account gives the archive a thread it can actually pull, which no other exhibit in this file does.

Crown Works delivered to an address. Delivery generates a carter's docket with a street on it, and carters keep their books for the tax office whatever their clients would prefer. The Chamberlain's ledger will not name the house. [[roll:4|The carrier's book will|because the carter was paid for carriage and night working — it is itemised on this very account — and a paid carter files a docket. The address exists in writing somewhere in the city.|carters' books from a coronation season are long gone.]]

Get the address. The file's title asks who signed and in what. This exhibit establishes **where**, which is the first of those three questions the archive has been able to answer with a document.

exhibits.onRecord: A posting slip for the ceremonial lantern post on the night of the account, reconstructed from what John Lee says he was issued and ordered: stand, light, salute the household, do not leave the post. Two clauses the account's night turns on — the dungeon detail amended from four to two, and a standing order that any guard found off post is to be walked down to the dungeon detail and left there. Prisoner held; no description to be given to the ceremonial establishment. The slip is signed for the Chamberlain, whose office [[roll:3|holds the keys|— and the account has the Chamberlain in a new suit telling a lantern post 'I have the keys to every door' an hour before the cell was found unlocked, which makes the signature line and the boast the same sentence twice|— which is the ordinary arrangement in any palace; the Chamberlain's office holds the household keys in every reign, and a guard's slip signed 'for the Chamberlain' is routine paper]].
exhibits.analysis:
## What the slip is and is not

It is a reconstruction and the exhibit says so twice. Waluigi did not recover a posting slip from 955 BF; he recovered a guard's account of being posted, and has written the slip the way the Captain's office would have written it, from the account's details, so that the file has a document to argue with instead of a paragraph. Every word of the two clauses that matter is a claim the account supports — the dungeon was thinly held enough for a lantern post to be sent to it, and the guards who found John Lee in a tower walked him down there without discussion, as though that were the order. The slip states the order. The account shows it being obeyed.

## Why the amendment matters more than the prisoner

The journals attributed to the Chamberlain say *the positions were cleared*. The Loyalists read that as Highsun 1 — the forty-seven minutes with nobody at the Royal Suite. Here is a position being cleared a month early: a dungeon detail cut in half on the night a Koopa sat in an unlocked cell waiting for Fawful. Either this is the rehearsal or the Arrangement cleared positions as a habit, and in both readings the forty-seven minutes stop being an anomaly and start being a method. [[roll:4|Count the Toads below|: two on detail, both of whom the account later places as John Lee's escort — which means the dungeon was empty of guards the moment they went up to fetch a lantern post from a tower, and the cell stood unlocked in a corridor with nobody in it for as long as that took|: the account names no numbers for the detail; two is the slip's figure, built from the two escorts, and a reader should treat it as the archive's arithmetic, not the palace's]].

## The standing order

*Any guard found off post is to be walked to the dungeon detail and left there.* Waluigi has thought about this clause more than any other paper in the file this year. It is not a punishment order — a palace punishes a wandering guard with a sergeant, not a dungeon. It is a funnel. Whoever wrote the night's orders wanted any Toad who was where he should not be delivered to the one place in the castle where everything that should not be was. That is either staggering carelessness or a design that assumed nobody would come back up the stairs. One did. He had a lantern.

## What it fails to prove

It does not name the Chamberlain. 'For the Chamberlain' is how every slip in every palace is signed and the son was in the building too. It does not prove the detail was cut *for* the handshake rather than for the broadcast. And it is a reconstruction, which means a hostile reader can refuse it entirely — and Waluigi has left them the room to, by marking it. What it proves is smaller and harder: that the account's night is internally consistent with a palace that had arranged its own guard, and that a guard who was arranged into the dungeon came out of it with a story nobody had planned for.

exhibits.onRecord: Thin shop stock, folded twice, scorched at one corner, six words in a hand the account did not recognise and no signature it mentions: *meet me in Fawful's bean shop*. Found by John Lee on a palace guard who had died in Bowser's fire in the hall — a Toad in livery, waiting with the rest of the hall for the Mario brothers — and found before anybody had said the words 'bean shop' to John Lee. He went to the address because the paper told him to. The Koopa, [[roll:4|who was there first|, had the shop's own card with 'do not bring the guard unless he has decided' on the back of it — so the shop expected a guard and did not expect this one; the letter in the dead Toad's coat was for somebody who had decided|, had left the dungeon by a route the account never saw and could have reached Toad Town by any door in the castle; nothing on the record makes the letter his]].
exhibits.analysis:
## The wrong pocket

Everything about the Arrangement, until this paper, lived below stairs: the dungeon, the unlocked cell, the hoods coming in from the dark end of a corridor. The letter is upstairs. It is in the coat of a palace guard standing in the hall, in livery, among the Toads, waiting for Mario. If the Arrangement had one Toad in the hall holding its address, it had more than one, and the hall that cheered the Guild a quarter of an hour later was not a hall of innocents being manipulated. It was a hall with its own people in it.

## Why the account's order matters

John Lee read the letter before anyone had mentioned the bean shop to him. That is the kind of detail a liar would not bother with and a guard would — because to the guard it is simply the reason he went where he went. For the file it is the whole chain of custody: the destination came from a dead Toad's pocket, not from Fawful, not from the Guild, not from the Koopa. Whoever wrote the six words wrote them for a palace guard, and a palace guard carried them into Bowser's fire without having gone. [[roll:5|Whether he was ever going to|: the slip was folded twice and scorched only at the corner, which is a note kept flat in a breast pocket for the length of a watch, not one read and discarded — he was carrying it to a time, and the time had not come|: the account cannot say; a note in a breast pocket is a note in a breast pocket, and guards keep all sorts of paper against their chests]].

## The hand

Not the guard's — the account was sure of that and nothing else. Waluigi will not name a writer from six words he has never seen. He will note that the Bean Badge's own shop card carries a second hand on its reverse, and that the capital file now holds two notes from the same night, in two hands, both routing people to one shop, one of them written before the night and one during it. A file that can put those two hands side by side can start asking who in the palace wrote letters for the shop.

## What it does not prove

That the dead guard was a conspirator. A note can be planted on a body; a note can be given to a Toad who did not know what the shop was. The letter proves the address was in the hall, and that is all it proves, and it is enough to move the Arrangement up one floor.

exhibits.onRecord: A trade card from the tray on the counter: beans of all nations, open before the castle wakes, one badge per loyal customer, *loyalty is decided by the proprietor*. On the reverse, in a different hand: *Back room. Bring the vial. Do not bring the guard unless he has decided.* The card is the shop's own voice and the back of it is a schedule — one that names the vial the Koopa was holding and a guard who had not yet decided, written before the guard came up through the grate. [[roll:3|Which guard|: the reverse was written for a Toad who would be brought, which is the dead guard's letter from the other side — somebody in the hall was expected at the shop and had not committed; the man who actually arrived was the one who had been shot at for not committing|: the card says 'the guard' and the night had a hall of them; the archive cannot say from the card alone which one the back room was waiting for]].
exhibits.analysis:
## A card with two hands on it

The front is Fawful. Nobody else writes *I HAVE BEANS* on a trade card and means it as a threat. The back is not Fawful: it is terse, it gives an order, it names an object and a condition, and it is written by somebody who had the authority to decide who came into the back room of Fawful's own shop. That is the Guild's hand or the Koopa's, and Waluigi leans Guild, because *do not bring the guard unless he has decided* is a sentence about recruitment, and the recruitment at dawn was conducted by the two operatives while Fawful explained a mushroom.

## 'Bring the vial'

The fat vial — the account's phrase — is the only object in the night that was built to go into somebody, and here it is on a shop card as a thing to be fetched. The vacuum shroom goes into Bowser by way of it; Fawful said so in the cloak. The card puts the vial on the Koopa's errand list *before* the dungeon, which means the plan for Bowser existed before Bowser came through the wall, which means the castle's warning about Bowser's attack — delivered, by his own admission, by the Koopa — was not a warning. It was a delivery schedule. [[roll:5|Read the hours line again|: 'the cellar does not keep hours' — a shop advertising, on its own card, that its cellar is open at all hours is a shop whose cellar is a door, and the drain the guard came up is the door it meant|: a bean shop with a cellar keeps stock in it, and a joke about hours on a trade card is a joke; the drain is in the account whatever the card says]].

## 'Unless he has decided'

The Guild wanted a guard who had chosen. Not a captured guard, not a frightened one — a decided one, because a Toad who has decided is a Toad who will stand a post on the right night and not jump. The hall's dead guard had the address and had not gone. John Lee arrived instead, having been shot at by the people writing the card, and was asked to join anyway, and was asked whether he was stupid when he wanted an escort. He had not decided. The card says he was not to be brought. He brought himself. The archive files that as the one thing in the night the Arrangement did not schedule.

## The limit

Waluigi has reproduced a card from an account's description of a tray. He has not held it. The front is reconstruction in the shop's voice; the reverse is the account's report of what the Koopa showed or said at the counter, rendered as the card the account describes. A reader is entitled to weigh that. Waluigi weighs it as the first piece of paper in the Arrangement file that was written by the Arrangement for its own use, rather than about it by its enemies afterwards.
